_meta.policy: Every real number in the game data points to one of these NASA pages by id. Anything without a source id is tagged designed (game balance) or derived (our formula on NASA numbers). Each page was opened and read on 2026-11-06; check them again before submission.

sources.title: NASA Mars Fact Sheet
sources.gives: Solar irradiance 586.2 W/m2; surface gravity 3.73 m/s2; mean surface pressure 6.36 mb (varies 4.0 to 8.7 mb); surface temperature mean about 214 K (-59 C), min 184 K (-89 C) and max 242 K (-31 C) at the Viking 1 site; solar day length 24.6597 hours.
sources.credit: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive

sources.title: NASA: Rover Results Include First Age Measurement on Mars and Help for Human Exploration
sources.gives: Curiosity RAD: average 0.67 millisieverts per day on the Mars surface, Aug 2012 to Jun 2013; round-trip dose for a human mission on the order of 1,000 millisieverts.

sources.title: Radiation Measurements on Mars (NASA Science)
sources.gives: Galactic cosmic rays contribute a slowly varying dose rate of about 210 micrograys per day on the Mars surface.

sources.title: Data From NASA Rover's Voyage to Mars Aids Planning (JPL)
sources.gives: Curiosity was exposed to an average of 1.8 millisieverts of galactic cosmic rays per day on its journey to Mars.

sources.title: Opportunity Hunkers Down During Dust Storm (JPL)
sources.gives: Estimated tau of 10.8 at Opportunity on 10 June 2018; the 2007 storm tau was above 5.5; storm first detected 30 May 2018; became planet-encircling 19 June 2018; began decaying 23 July 2018; rover temperature about -29 C on 10 June.

sources.title: PIA22930 Last Images Opportunity Took
sources.gives: Pancam images from 10 June 2018 (sol 5,111): faint Sun in the dust storm; tau about 10.8.

sources.title: PIA22737 Mars Climate Sounder Studies 2018 Dust Storm
sources.gives: Tau is a measure of how much light dust blocks; a tau of three means only about 5 percent of the sunlight entering the atmosphere directly reaches the surface. Storm: complex growth over the first month, near the peak for three weeks, then a multi-month decay.

sources.title: NASA GISS Mars24 Sunclock: Mars Landers
sources.gives: Curiosity at Gale Crater: 137.44 E, 4.59 S. Opportunity at Meridiani Planum: 354.47 E, -1.95 (latitude as printed).

sources.title: Mars Science Laboratory / Curiosity Fact Sheet (PDF)
sources.gives: Landing site 4.6 S, 137.4 E; elevation minus 4,501 meters; landing 6 Aug 2012 UT.

sources.title: Glacial Ice Deposits in Mid-Latitudes of Mars (PIA12861)
sources.gives: Image centred at 42.2 N, 24.7 E in Deuteronilus Mensae.

sources.title: Arcadia Planitia - False Color (NASA Science)
sources.gives: Image location listed as latitude 38.855, longitude 172.318 (positive east).

sources.title: NASA's Treasure Map for Water Ice on Mars
sources.gives: Water ice lies underground throughout the mid-latitudes; a large part of Arcadia Planitia is the most tempting northern target, with ice less than one foot (30 cm) below the surface in places and warmer-colored areas over two feet (60 cm) deep; you could use a shovel.

sources.title: Availability of Subsurface Water-Ice Resources in the Northern Mid-Latitudes of Mars (NASA NTRS 20205008958)
sources.gives: SWIM composite ice-consistency maps: the broad plains of Arcadia and the glacial networks across Deuteronilus Mensae match the greatest number of remote-sensing criteria for accessible ice-rich subsurface material. Morgan et al., Nature Astronomy 2021.

sources.title: Where Should Future Astronauts Land on Mars? Follow the Water (JPL)
sources.gives: Names the plains of Arcadia Planitia and glacier-filled valleys in Deuteronilus Mensae; northern mid-latitudes offer favorable elevations for landing.

sources.title: PIA16913 Steady Temperatures at Mars' Gale Crater
sources.gives: REMS air temperature at Gale: daily highs about 0 C and lows about -70 C, mid-Aug 2012 to late Feb 2013.

sources.title: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief: ECLSS (OCHMO)
sources.gives: Oxygen: 0.771 kg per person per day at rest, 1.083 kg with exercise (75 kg crewmember); drinking water minimum 2.5 L per crewmember per day; average 3,035 kcal per crewmember per day.
sources.credit: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer

sources.title: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief: Water (OCHMO)
sources.gives: Minimum 2.5 L per crewmember per day for drinking and food rehydration; hygiene water is mission dependent (no number given).
sources.credit: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer

sources.title: Astronaut Mass Balance for Long Duration Missions (NASA NTRS 20190027563, ICES-2019-126)
sources.gives: Reference astronaut (82 kg, 90 min exercise per day): oxygen 0.89 kg per day; drinking water 2.79 kg; as-packaged food 2.39 kg (ISS planning value from the Baseline Values and Assumptions Document); CO2 produced 1.08 kg.

sources.title: PIA22487 Mars Before and After Dust Storm
sources.gives: MRO MARCI views of Mars in May and July 2018 (published 19 July 2018).

sources.title: PIA22519 2018 Giant Dust Storm on Mars
sources.gives: MRO images 31 May to 11 June 2018 showing the storm spreading (published 13 June 2018).

sources.title: PIA22929 Opportunity's Last Message
sources.gives: Last image Opportunity sent, 10 June 2018 (sol 5,111), Pancam left eye, mostly dark from the dust storm.

sources.title: PIA22521 Shades of Martian Darkness
sources.gives: Simulated views of a darkening Martian sky at tau 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11.

sources.title: Mars' Surface Radiation Environment Measured with the MSL Curiosity Rover (NASA NTRS 20180007641)
sources.gives: Citation record: Hassler et al., Science 343 (6169), 2014, doi:10.1126/science.1244797. Covers galactic cosmic rays and solar energetic particles over 300 days from 7 Aug 2012.

sources.title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines
sources.gives: Rules for using NASA images and media (credit NASA; the NASA insignia and logotype are not free to use).
